item.text: {"question_id":"4B.4","answer":"During 2023, courts and the INE remained capable of constraining the executive: the Supreme Court invalidated the National Guard’s transfer of operational, administrative, budgetary, organizational, functional, and command control to Defense, and its suspension enabled the INE to halt Plan B implementation and retain prior electoral rules. The institutional record is nevertheless mixed. López Obrador’s administration pursued the military transfer, publicly criticized courts, and executive authorities pressured judges; the Working Group also reported judicial budget cuts and continuing detention-related failures. Autonomous oversight bodies were weakened by delayed or vetoed appointments and budget pressure: INAI could not initially function with four of seven commissioners and accumulated nearly 6,000 pending cases, while IFT remained without a full board. Attribution is not uniform: Senate failures and other appointing authorities shared responsibility, and the record does not establish the president’s personal control over every blockage. The Supreme Court later allowed INAI to meet with four commissioners, López Obrador complied with the COFECE appointment order, and the government invited the UN Working Group, which reported full and unimpeded access and cooperation. Thus, formal courts and election oversight could constrain the ruler, but their independence and operational capacity faced substantial executive pressure; the evidence does not establish full compliance with the National Guard ruling during the target period.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0005-E001","BATCH-0009-E001","BATCH-0010-E005","BATCH-0026-E020","BATCH-0043-E010","BATCH-0049-E011","BATCH-0055-E006","BATCH-0055-E008","BATCH-0014-E002","BATCH-0004-E009"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0010-E011","BATCH-0013-E004","BATCH-0018-E015","BATCH-0026-E014","BATCH-0031-E013","BATCH-0041-E008","BATCH-0055-E004","BATCH-0055-E012","BATCH-0057-E007","BATCH-0057-E017"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The evidence does not establish the extent or timing of López Obrador’s compliance with the National Guard ruling; one later account reports nonimplementation, while the supplied court and contemporary reports do not resolve the issue.","Appointment blockages involved the president, Senate, Morena legislators, and different appointing authorities; presidential responsibility is therefore issue-specific rather than uniform.","The UN Working Group’s findings were preliminary and covered federal, state, and municipal authorities, so they do not assign López Obrador personal responsibility for every reported failure.","The supplied record gives limited direct evidence on tenure protection, court funding decisions beyond reported cuts, auditors, and local-government autonomy. "],"corrections_made":["Recast alleged National Guard noncompliance as unresolved rather than established fact.","Narrowed attribution for INAI, IFT, COFECE, and other appointment blockages to the actors identified by the evidence.","Added the UN Working Group’s invitation, full and unimpeded access, cooperation, and acknowledged institutional reforms as material contrary evidence.","Distinguished formal institutional constraints from de facto pressure and operational impairment.","Removed unsupported claims that all appointment failures were directly attributable to López Obrador or that every cited institution was uniformly unable to function."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["If the target period requires a definitive finding on post-ruling National Guard implementation, obtain direct contemporaneous implementation evidence.","Reopen if the full ledger contains evidence on auditors, local governments, court tenure, or funding that materially changes the institutional pattern.","Reopen if additional evidence resolves whether executive pressure on judges was systematic, personally directed, or primarily attributable to lower-level authorities."]}
